title: Optimization and certification of Max-Cut in random cubic graphs
formal:
Determine the two-valued function \(F:\{\mathrm{optimization},\mathrm{certification}\}\to\mathbb R\) for Max-Cut on a uniformly random simple labeled \(3\)-regular graph:
\[
F(\mathrm{optimization})=a_*\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(\mathrm{certification})=b_*.
\]
Here \(a_*\) is the supremum of asymptotic cut sizes achievable with high probability by uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms, and \(b_*\) is the infimum of asymptotic upper bounds obtainable with high probability by uniform randomized polynomial-time producers of always sound, polynomial-time-verifiable certificates. Both values count crossing edges per vertex. The definitions below fix the quantifiers without assuming that either computational optimum is attained.

This is the user-approved specialization, recorded on 16 September 2026, of the source’s broader program for unspecified sparse random CSP models. The general model parameter is deliberately replaced by this single distribution and this pair of optimal computational thresholds.

source_formulation.text: For a sparse random CSP model, how close to its optimal value can efficient algorithms construct assignments and efficiently certify upper bounds?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the general program on p. 97:2. The card specializes it to random cubic Max-Cut and two computational thresholds with explicit user approval on 16 September 2026; this specialized formulation is not a quotation from the source.

why: Random cubic Max-Cut is a concrete sparse optimization model in which excellent solutions and convincing upper certificates may have different computational limits. Determining both thresholds would measure that gap in a fixed distribution, test the limits of spectral and local methods, and clarify which information about a typical optimum can be made into an efficient proof for an individual instance.
status_note: The approved specialized target is fully specified. The original 2022 paper poses the broader program; 2024 work gives conjecture-dependent certification hardness and a March 2026 preprint reports an improved cubic upper bound. This bounded review found no unconditional determination of both computational extrema to the required precision. The numerical LP certificate was not independently validated, and its printed discretization inequality has the local defect described in context. Status remains uncertain rather than asserting that the exact new benchmark is independently certified open or resolved.

progress.text: The basic semidefinite relaxation for random regular Max-Cut is shown to have a precise asymptotic value, recalled in the source’s §1.1. This settles that relaxation rather than all polynomial-time algorithms.
The Ising-antiferromagnet analysis proves a variational upper bound on the true typical maximum cut, with a cubic numerical evaluation in Table 1.
Noisy-lift detection hardness is proposed as an explanation for certification gaps; the cubic certification obstruction depends on this conjecture.
Version 7 reports an improved cubic certification upper bound through a finite linear program. This review records both the claim and the limits of its verification.
The user approves specializing the previously unspecified random-CSP program to the pair of optimal construction and certification thresholds for uniform simple random cubic graphs.

importance.reason: A canonical sparse random optimization problem separating the ability to find good solutions from the ability to certify their quality, with concrete links to average-case hardness, spectral relaxations and statistical physics.
importance.basis: Individual review of the user-approved cubic specialization, its two distinct computational extrema, the original random-CSP program, true-optimum bounds and recent conditional certification results.

sentences: The user has specialized the general random-CSP program to Max-Cut on uniform simple random cubic graphs.
The target is the pair of best polynomial-time cut-construction and always sound certification thresholds, measured in crossing edges per vertex.
Randomized uniform algorithms must meet their performance guarantees with probability tending to one, while certificates must remain sound on every graph.
Known spectral values, true-optimum bounds, conditional hardness and a recent reported certification improvement do not establish both requested unconditional thresholds.
A complete answer supplies approximations to both constants within absolute error one hundredth and proves their correctness in Lean.

definitions:
For every even integer \(n\geq4\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on the labeled vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with degree exactly three at every vertex. There are no loops or parallel edges, and disconnected graphs are allowed. Let \(\mu_n\) be the uniform distribution on \(\mathcal G_n\). All limits below run through even \(n\) tending to infinity. The graph is given explicitly by a unary size header and the upper triangle of its adjacency matrix, so its input length \(L\) is of order \(n^2\). Algorithms receive this graph, without access to a sampling oracle. Invalid encodings are rejected in polynomial time.

A cut is any vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\), with no balance constraint. Its value and the maximum cut value are
\[
q_G(x)=\frac{|\{\{i,j\}\in E(G):x_i\ne x_j\}|}{n},\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(G)=\max_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}q_G(x).
\]
Thus values belong to \([0,3/2]\). A cut containing a fraction \(\theta\) of all edges has value \(3\theta/2\), since \(|E(G)|=3n/2\). The benchmark tolerance is applied in these per-vertex units, not to an approximation ratio and not to the fraction of edges.

Polynomial time means worst-case bit complexity on a uniform multitape Turing machine: for each algorithm there are fixed integers \(C,k\geq1\) bounding its steps by \(C(L+1)^k\) on every valid graph and every random-bit sequence. Randomness consists of independent fair bits, at most as many as the time bound allows, independently of the input graph. Finite programs have no advice or oracles. Deterministic algorithms are included. Reading and writing rational numbers, outputting a cut or a certificate, and all precision used in numerical computation count toward the bound. Constants and exponents may depend on the algorithm, but not on \(n\), the graph or its random bits.

An optimization algorithm \(A\) always outputs a valid cut. A level \(a\in[0,3/2]\) is achievable if there is one such polynomial-time algorithm satisfying, for every rational \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n\ \mathrm{even}}}
\Pr_{G\sim\mu_n,\,\rho}\big[q_G(A(G;\rho))\geq a-\varepsilon\big]=1.
\]
Define \(a_*\) as the supremum of these levels. Here \(\rho\) denotes the algorithm’s random bits. The tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is a performance quantifier, not an additional input. The definition optimizes over all finite uniform algorithms; it does not require the supremum to be achieved by one algorithm.

A certification scheme is a pair \((P,V)\). The producer \(P\) is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a rational number \(u\in[0,3/2]\) and a binary certificate \(\pi\). Write rationals as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. Both output lengths are polynomial in \(L\). The verifier \(V\) is deterministic and runs in time polynomial in the total bit length of \((G,u,\pi)\). It rejects malformed encodings. Soundness is universal:
\[
V(G,u,\pi)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{OPT}(G)\leq u
\]
for every valid cubic graph \(G\), every rational \(u\in[0,3/2]\) and every finite certificate \(\pi\). In particular, soundness cannot fail on rare graphs or rare random choices. The producer must always return an accepted pair on every valid input and every random-bit sequence; the trivial bound \(u=3/2\) may be used as a fallback. Producing the certificate efficiently is part of the target, not just verifying an existentially supplied short certificate.

A level \(b\in[0,3/2]\) is certifiable if there is one such scheme satisfying, for every rational \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\lim_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n\ \mathrm{even}}}
\Pr_{G\sim\mu_n,\,\rho}\big[u(P(G;\rho))\leq b+\varepsilon\big]=1.
\]
Define \(b_*\) as the infimum of these levels. The notation \(u(P(G;\rho))\) selects the numerical bound from the producer’s output. No particular proof system, semidefinite relaxation or local algorithm is imposed. The algorithms and their verifiers can vary when taking the infimum, which need not be attained.

These extrema are well defined. The all-edge upper bound gives a certification scheme. Repeatedly moving a vertex that has fewer than two crossing incident edges strictly increases the cut; after at most \(3n/2\) moves the resulting cut has at least \(n\) crossing edges. This gives a polynomial-time baseline \(a_*\geq1\). Every cut is at most every accepted upper bound on the same graph, and the two high-probability events intersect with probability tending to one. Consequently \(1\leq a_*\leq b_*\leq3/2\). No existence theorem for a limit of \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) is needed to define the two computational extrema.

context_blocks.text: The original source leaves the random CSP model unspecified. This card formerly recorded that missing choice as pending specification. The user selected Max-Cut on random 3-regular graphs and asked for the best asymptotic polynomial-time construction and certification quality. The fixed distribution, normalization, randomization convention and certificate model above make that approved narrower objective explicit; other CSP predicates, densities and degree distributions remain part of the broader source program.

Finding a cut and certifying an upper bound solve different computational tasks. A proposed cut is easy to evaluate. A claimed upper bound must rule out every possible cut, so an algorithm that finds excellent solutions can coexist with a much weaker efficiently obtainable upper certificate. The true typical optimum lies between these kinds of guarantees, but knowing its typical value alone does not produce an always sound certificate on a particular input.

The standard spectral bound uses the adjacency matrix \(A_G\). If a rational \(t\) satisfies \(tI+A_G\succeq0\), then \(x^\top A_Gx\geq-tn\) for every cut vector, and \(q_G(x)\leq3/4+t/4\). Positive semidefiniteness means that the symmetric matrix has nonnegative quadratic form on every real vector; it can be checked with exact rational linear algebra and polynomial bit complexity. Rational approximation from above to \(-\lambda_{\min}(A_G)\) therefore gives a sound, efficiently produced certificate. The random regular spectral theorem yields the asymptotic level \(3/4+\sqrt2/2\), approximately \(1.457107\). The source also records that the basic SDP relaxation has this limit; a tight value for that relaxation is not optimality among all certification methods.

Information-theoretic bounds concern the maximum cut itself. Coja-Oghlan and coauthors prove a variational upper bound whose displayed cubic numerical value is approximately \(0.9241\) of all edges, or \(1.38615\) per vertex. The variational theorem, not an unqualified rounding of that decimal, is the rigorous statement. It bounds the quality of any constructed cut on typical inputs, but the probabilistic theorem does not by itself certify a bound for every individual input graph.

Kunisky and Yu propose that it is hard to distinguish a uniform random regular graph from a slightly perturbed random lift of a suitable small Ramanujan graph. A lift replaces each base vertex by a fiber and each base edge by a matching between fibers; a Ramanujan graph has its nontrivial adjacency eigenvalues bounded in magnitude by \(2\sqrt{d-1}\). Their detection conjecture gives a conditional obstruction to certifying cubic Max-Cut below \(17/18\) of the edges, namely \(17/12\) per vertex. This is a conjecture-dependent computational lower bound, not an unconditional lower bound proved here. Applying a detection hypothesis to the randomized producer class above requires its randomized-test version; a deterministic-only hypothesis cannot silently replace it.

The March 2026 version of Nagda, Raghavan and Thakurta reports a polynomial-time certification upper bound of \(0.953\) of the edges, or \(1.4295\) per vertex, using local cut distributions and spectral constraints in a fixed finite linear program. Its cubic lower bound remains the earlier conjecture-dependent one. The numerical linear-program certificate was not independently verified in this review. Moreover, the printed discretized lower inequality in Lemma B.3 fails for an empty cut with grid value zero and positive discretization width: it asks for a correlation larger than one. This is a local defect in the displayed argument that may be repairable; it is not a refutation of the reported theorem. The number is recorded as reported progress, not as an independently certified conclusion or a determination of \(b_*\).

Degree three stays fixed as the number of vertices grows. Results that become near-optimal only as the degree tends to infinity, bounds for dense random graphs, and worst-case approximation guarantees have different quantifiers. Likewise, a certificate whose correctness only holds with high probability over the graph is weaker than the always sound, efficiently obtainable certificates required here.

quality_review.scope: Checked target, definitions, quantifiers, answer criterion, context, significance and dated source claims. Bounded later-work checks do not independently certify every cited proof.

answer_criterion:
Supply an explicit function \(g:\{\mathrm{optimization},\mathrm{certification}\}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[
|g(\mathrm{optimization})-a_*|\leq\frac1{100},\qquad
|g(\mathrm{certification})-b_*|\leq\frac1{100}.
\]
Two rational approximations or two unambiguous mathematical expressions are valid ways to supply \(g\). Certified intervals of width at most \(1/50\) for both extrema qualify through their midpoints. A restatement of the definitions of \(a_*\) and \(b_*\) without determining approximations or certified intervals is not an answer. Exact evaluation is welcome but not required.

Both sides of each interval must be justified for the full algorithm classes and the specified graph distribution. Constructing a good cut only gives a lower bound on \(a_*\); constructing a good certificate only gives an upper bound on \(b_*\). Their opposite bounds require valid limitations, possibly derived from information-theoretic bounds, on every algorithm or scheme in the class. All claims must be unconditional: an unproved complexity or detection conjecture does not discharge the Lean target. Simulations, predictions for the typical true optimum, the exact value of one SDP relaxation, or hardness confined to one algorithm family do not alone determine both entries of \(F\). Numerical estimates must retain enough exact or certified arithmetic to prove the stated absolute error.
